I just finished my first play through of the game and got what I can assume is the expected good ending. Given the gallery, there seems to be multiple types of endings.

This was... short. Much shorter than 2.

I have about 15 hours in Simulacra 2 while this took 3 hours to finish.

That being said, this was because the puzzles and sleuthing required in Simulacra 2 was more obscure and multiparted than what is presented in 3. The to do list was more hints and solutions than just minor quests this time around as it was more specific and broken into far more steps for greater clarity. This made the game much faster to go through as you almost always knew what to do next and could get huge help from the people you were speaking with. Perhaps this was feedback from how 2 was too obscure and some people felt like they spent hours looking for something entirely not obvious to them so this was added to help with it.

I can see it helping but it made it feel like I really wasnt needed. All these people had literally the answers themselves and all i had was someones phone. Any one else could have figured it out where as in 2 I felt like only I COULD solve it.

The feed has been streamlined and what you unlock instead is barfed at you in large chunks instead of the steady trickle that you get from social media sleuthing like in 2. This however made everything feel less personal. I didnt care about the missing people at all since they had nothing else going for them identity wise. They were footnotes pushed in to move the story along.

There doesnt seem to be a lot of character in this one. Pacing with the characters seem incredibly jarring as you go from casual work associates to suddenly having to answer deep mental health trauma in scenarios that come from left field and not in a natural way. The social media aspects were very lacking as you couldnt explore much except a small town feed.

Its easy to describe a story as 4 acts. The hook, the crescendo, the reveal, then the resolution.

I didnt feel like there was a lot of build up. The hook is the crescendo itself. Going into game knowing people are missing already was not really that interesting. Before I knew it, I found myself collecting pieces to finish the "ritual" to solve the problem. This also did not feel like I was apart of the story or had much agency. All the pieces were given to me because i asked someone nicely. A relationship that was already built by someone I never meet. I take advantage of all his work, his relationships, and his findings, just to ask other people to do the big bits for me. I never perform any of the rituals, I never do any of the fighting, I am way more of a casual observer than someone who held anyone's fate in my hands.

The ending left me really bored as I truly didnt feel what the relationship was between any of the people. The premise is a bit wonky as its a shut in PI type that just made esoteric relationships with various people around town that suddenly become holders of big puzzle pieces.

I am guessing due to pandemic, the development had to cut back because there doesnt seem to be a giant web of possibilities like 2 did, there are very straight cut and dry of live or die decisions and I kept feeling like I could have messed up everything when the wording between two dialogue options were basically the same and you had only 3 seconds to choose.

Some of the UI and UX were confusing. The minigame felt incredibly easy but that made me question if I was getting baited into something but instead it really was just simply as it was presented. It was more tedious than fun because you had to watch some really weird forced acting as you played the truck guy in phasmophobia on a far smaller scale essentially. 

Not as good as 2. Still recommend because it was enjoyable but definitely a weaker production in comparison.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra 3, developed by Kaigan Games and published by Neon Doctrine, continues the found-phone horror tradition established by its predecessors, delivering an immersive narrative experience centered around digital mystery and psychological suspense. Set in the eerie town of Stonecreek, the game places players in the role of an intern at a local newspaper tasked with assisting investigative journalist Ruby Myers. The central mystery revolves around the disappearance of Paul Castillo, a software developer whose phone becomes the gateway to unraveling the secrets behind his vanishing. By exploring his digital life through texts, photos, videos, and various apps, players are drawn into a chilling tale that combines supernatural elements with a realistic portrayal of modern technology, creating a sense of intimacy and urgency that few horror games achieve.

The gameplay is built around interacting with Paul's smartphone, where every notification, message, and multimedia file serves as a piece of the puzzle. Players navigate through different apps, decode cryptic information, and use hacking mechanics to access deeper layers of the mystery. The real-time progression of events adds tension and immediacy, encouraging quick decisions that influence the unfolding story. This dynamic storytelling approach allows multiple branching endings based on player choices, enhancing replay value and inviting players to revisit the narrative to uncover all possible outcomes. The interface cleverly mimics a real phone’s UI, making the experience feel personal and immersive, as if players are genuinely investigating a missing person’s digital footprint.

Visually, Simulacra 3 stays true to the series' minimalist yet effective design, presenting a realistic smartphone interface filled with authentic-looking apps and multimedia content. The integration of live-action video calls and interactive elements boosts immersion, while the sound design subtly heightens the suspense throughout the investigation. Despite these strengths, some players have found certain puzzles to be ambiguous or overly obscure, which can stall progression and disrupt the narrative flow. The pacing, while deliberately methodical to build atmosphere, may feel slow to those expecting more traditional horror gameplay or quicker resolutions.

Critical reception for Simulacra 3 has been varied, reflecting its niche appeal. While some reviewers praise its atmospheric storytelling, innovative use of the found-phone format, and the effective blend of horror with investigative mechanics, others point out shortcomings in character depth and the occasional frustration with puzzle design. The player community echoes this division, with many appreciating the eerie mood and unique narrative delivery but expressing disappointment over certain gameplay limitations and the game's pacing. For fans of narrative-driven horror and those intrigued by the concept of piecing together stories through digital clues, Simulacra 3 offers a compelling experience, though it may not resonate with everyone.

In summary, Simulacra 3 represents a strong continuation of the found-phone horror genre, delivering a haunting and interactive story that makes clever use of modern technology as a storytelling device. Its immersive atmosphere and branching narrative paths offer a deep dive into mystery and supernatural horror, appealing especially to players who enjoy investigative and choice-driven games. While some gameplay elements and pacing choices might divide opinion, the game stands as a noteworthy title for those looking to explore a psychologically tense and digitally immersive horror experience.

Rating: 6/10

The game feels unfinished. 

I went into this game with high hopes. Starts off like 1 and 2, you get a phone under weird circumstances. 
This one however is different. There is a lot of mechanics they teach you along the way. That they just use 1 time. There is a perfect sequence to use the trace mechanic, instead they chose to use a "Dark Mode" mechanic out of no where, that had no tutorial. (this took me 30 minutes to figure out) 

The phone experience is just weird on 3. No real personality to the phone. Even after you unlock the texts, feels bland, doesn't feel like a phone that any human had used ever. 

The story is fine, build up is weird and the pacing is odd. 

I would give it a try, but 3 is just not as suspenseful as the first 2 entries in the series.

review_text_raw:
I really wanted to like this game, I really did. 

I loved the previous Simulacra titles, I loved what they did, how they tackled topics of online life from a very different perspective, I loved the variety of characters and the decisions you got to make about them. And mostly, it was just incredibly fun stalking through someone's phone, through social media, seeing other people react to things in realtime, it wasn't 100% convincing, but it made all of it feel a lot more real. And I loved the feeling of danger when getting in contact and confronting the Entities yourself, it was engaging and scary and amazing storytelling.

All of this is gone here.

Let's start with the concept, the previous titles revolved around some current digital topics, online dating, influencers or predatory games. This game mostly drops the digital. It's a ghost story in a town followed through a Maps-App. There's so many topics that could've fit amazingly - NFT's, VR, AR, even Covid and being forced to be home (which admittedly does come up but in a shallow and meaningless way). But we got a Maps-App and a town-mystery, with themes of power, government, community and the interaction of urban myth and history. This too could potentially have been something interesting, but no. 

The story is maybe the most okay part about this game, the town myth is set up nicely, but quite basic, there are some interesting twists and misdirections, and I loved the part about how all of the events started [spoiler]Amy is just a really cool and interesting character[/spoiler]. But many parts absolutely do not work. Some are really forced like [spoiler]when we have to decieve the poor receptionist and cost her her job because Ruby didn't tell us what she was going to do[/spoiler] and the story also doesn't get nearly enough breathing room to work. Especially because you have to work with different characters and convince them of things, yet you've barely interacted before. It doesn't feel like you're participating in a story but playing a bad puzzle game.

The characters are okay-ish, the one you're interacting most with is Ruby and she's written as though you're meant to form a connection, but I just didn't, I didn't feel that much for her or care that much about her, so the emotional core that's built around her just doesn't work. There are some other characters I liked a lot more like [spoiler]Persephone / Damien and Carin[/spoiler] they're fun interacting with and they have personality, but they're also barely there. And even them are just lame compared to the fun interactions with Murillo or unhinged rants of Aria in Simulacra 2, who just felt like real people, with their own desires, hopes, dreams and delusions.

The horror / scary parts are just completely gone. It's so sad, the previous parts could pull you in so much, through the phone glitching or asking invasive or interesting questions, and create a real sense of dread, but here you don't ever feel in danger, because you never are. How would you feel in danger if the Beldam works by [spoiler]ppl seeing graffiti that wasn't there before, or encountering that eye symbol[/spoiler] which are mostly just tied to the real world. Nothing is i.e. indicating you've forgotten time, like that could've been a great point of tension, like a glitch followed by Ruby calling you and asking where you've been the last days. But nothing interesting or scary happens to you. I'd say the most tense sequence was [spoiler]getting Ruby out of Paul's House[/spoiler] but even there you weren't under time pressure, you didn't have to account for it moving, it wasn't challenging at all. Like [spoiler]electronics drew in the Beldam, her phone could've slowly drawn the Beldam towards her unless you activated something else[/spoiler]. And the Beldam itself isn't scary either. The previous Simulacra were always abstract, unfathomable, which made them scary and interesting, but giving the Beldam a bad CGI form didn't do the "horror" any favors. 

The mechanics in the game and the puzzles were also just lame. Most of it is very bland and unoriginal and the Atlas app (maps) is probably the worst of all. It's such a hacked together mess that doesn't make sense as a piece of software, especially the tracking function, and the hints in that function just make everything a lot worse. Like [spoiler]Thomas favorite place gives you the hint with the coffee order. At first I thought, hey there's this dude rating the Beldam locations, maybe I have to bring that in order? Nope. It says something about chronology, maybe I have to sort the ratings by the date posted? Nope. Oh it says something about a specific order in the description, I saw the post like that (@leftOnRead) might it be the places from which this account posted in order? Nope. What I didn't know was that I wasn't far enough and didn't have the grind, park and bus stop on the map yet.[/spoiler] I wasted so much time because of the hint system trying to solve something I couldn't yet.

The previous titles made you feel smart for figuring stuff out, piecing it together, hacking into things, especially because you had a "real phone", from another person, where you just had to circumvent things, but this game does the horrible mistake of dropping all pretenses. It's not a phone from a person missing, it's a puzzle box by a nerd who doesn't wanna give you straightforward information. There's nothing personal in there. NOTHING. No photos, no chats, everything is locked in his fun juiced up Atlas version. You don't try to outsmart technology to gather hidden intel, you have to get around the tedious roadblocks put in place by the informant - why, exactly? At first it's framed like he only had time to send the phone, but then WHY did he make the effort of hiding everything in these tedious puzzles? Especially when he wanted the information to get out and Ruby able to act. The "social media" (everything you get is the social page on the Atlas app) is sadly also incredibly sparse. There's a few posts you can go through, but where in S2 these mattered and you got to know more about the characters and some characters you would later interact with, here in S3 they barely matter at all. They're not engaging to read through, nor interesting discusssions, they're just lame filler. All of the fun of peeking into someone else's life is gone.

I want to have a small aside about presentation, I guess it was produced under Covid and therefore limited and basically all of it is made with greenscreen and really bad integration. The lighting doesn't match properly, the greenscreen is badly keyed and the acting is okay at best, but these are all things I could've forgiven for an interesting, scary, fun, engaging story. They try to do a lot of 3D stuff where the previous games stuck with 2D effects that worked a lot better, because they don't have the budget to do the 3D right.

Then let's finally come to the ending. Navigating the situation was very confusing. [spoiler]You basically have to talk Ruby down to her senses but I had no idea which answers and which reactions meant what. Sometimes she breaks out in this red demonic voice, but it's unclear if that is supposed to be the entity taking more or getting less control.[/spoiler] I had no idea what was going on and even thought I had failed just to discover I actually got the best ending. All of it is then quickly wrapped up, but it fails to leave anything behind about its themes. Everything is magically fine, or everything is incredibly doomed, it's just as empty as the myth of the Beldam itself. It's really sad to see a series I held in very high regard fall off so steeply.

review_text_raw:
This is a very soft recommend. 

I'm a big fan of the first two games and this phone detective genre as a whole and I was very excited for this game when it came out, but had put it on hold for some other games I was playing and finally got through it this morning. 

Bullet points incoming: 

- The game itself is just okay. The story is serviceable but isn't as compelling as 1 or 2, as none of the characters really stood out. They just mostly served as quick conversation pieces and possible plot points / beats on your journey rather than actual characters. It's nothing bad, but the severe lack of personality from most of the characters is just a bit of a letdown. 

- Gameplay was good, but definitely not as great as previous iterations. I personally didn't mind the more linear aspect of it (sure more puzzles would've been a lot better), but I felt for what it was doing it hit the mark so to speak.

- I know some people missed the horror element of it, but in reality a lot of the horror elements from the first 2 were cheap jumpscares which honestly I'm glad are gone bc that's all they are. Cheap ways to scare you and make you go BOO. That being said, the lack of ambient noise / other creepy subtle things from the first 2 games are also toned way down, to where this isn't really a horror game to me, but more of a mystery / adventure game. I feel going into it in that mindset may help more.

- Also, just curious, why would you remove the fast text option from Simulacra 2 for any subsequent playthroughs? That made being able to replay the game (if you so choose to or to achievement hunt) WAY easier and tolerable since you didn't have to wait for the slow pacing of the texts to come in. Removing that seems like such a huge misstep and is likely the only reason I won't 100% this one like I did the others bc in total reality, this is the first simulacra game where I don't really feel like trying to go back and do it.

All in all, is the game bad?
No, but it's nothing amazing either.

Is it a step down from the previous 2?
Yes.

Is it a horror game?
In my opinion, no. Consider this one more of a mystery / thriller experience versus horror. 

Would I recommend it?
If you liked the other 2 games, I think you'll still at least enjoy your time enough to get through it once. If you don't like the previous 2, you probably won't care for it and I'd skip it. If you're in the middle, get it on sale and give a try maybe. If you don't like it, you can always return it before the 2 hour mark.

That made being able to replay the game (if you so choose to or to achievement hunt) WAY easier and tolerable since you didn't have to wait for the slow pacing of the texts to come in. Removing that seems like such a huge misstep and is likely the only reason I won't 100% this one like I did the others bc in total reality, this is the first simulacra game where I don't really feel like trying to go back and do it. All in all, is the game bad? No, but it's nothing amazing either. Is it a step down from the previous 2? Yes. Is it a horror game? In my opinion, no. Consider this one more of a mystery / thriller experience versus horror. Would I recommend it? If you liked the other 2 games, I think you'll still at least enjoy your time enough to get through it once. If you don't like the previous 2, you probably won't care for it and I'd skip it. If you're in the middle, get it on sale and give a try maybe. If you don't like it, you can always return it before the 2 hour mark.
